opus-5.5.text:
I think the way to see it is that architecture innovation sits right at the intersection of algorithms and systems, and you can't really separate the two anymore.

On the algorithm side, the core question with something like linear attention is about expressiveness versus efficiency. Standard softmax attention is very powerful because every token can look at every other token with full precision, but the cost grows quadratically with sequence length. Linear attention, and related ideas like state space models or various recurrent formulations, compress the history into a fixed-size state. That's much cheaper, but you lose something. The model has to decide what to remember and what to forget. So for a long time, the algorithmic research was really about how to close that quality gap: better gating, better decay mechanisms, delta-rule style updates, and so on. And what we've seen recently is that the gap has narrowed quite a lot, especially when you use hybrid designs that mix a few full attention layers with many linear layers.

But I'd argue the systems side is just as important, maybe more so in practice. An architecture only matters if it runs efficiently on real hardware. Transformers won partly because they map extremely well onto GPUs: big matrix multiplications, highly parallel training. Many earlier recurrent ideas were elegant on paper but couldn't be trained efficiently at scale. A lot of the recent progress in linear attention came from people figuring out chunk-wise parallel algorithms and writing kernels that actually saturate the hardware. Without that, the theoretical complexity advantage doesn't translate into wall-clock speed.

Why does this matter now? Because the demands on models have changed. With long reasoning chains, agents, long context, and multimodal inputs, especially video, sequence lengths are exploding. Inference cost becomes the bottleneck, and the KV cache in standard attention becomes a huge memory burden. So efficiency isn't just a nice optimization anymore; it determines what kinds of capabilities you can even afford to build.

So my view is that architecture innovation is essentially co-design. You ask what the model needs to represent, what the hardware is good at, and what the workload looks like, and you look for designs that satisfy all three. Linear attention is interesting not because it's a magic replacement for the Transformer, but because it's one of the clearest examples of the field rethinking that balance as the workload shifts toward very long sequences.

r001.rationale: The response describes architecture as co-design at the intersection of algorithms, systems, and workloads; it does not state that architectural choices are subordinate to algorithmic and systems needs.

r002.rationale: It does not discuss an algorithm that avoids backpropagating through history or say that such an algorithm would make linear attention unnecessary.

r003.rationale: It does not suggest that a successful no-backpropagation approach would eliminate the distinction between training and inference phases.

r004.rationale: It mentions chunk-wise parallel algorithms and linear attention’s compressed state, but does not explain that its separable recurrent structure enables parallelizing next-token prediction.

fable-5.1.text:
That's a question I think about a lot, because I came up through the architecture side. ResNet, ShuffleNet, those were all architecture work, so I have a natural bias here that I try to correct for.

My honest view today is that architecture is important, but it's not the main story anymore. If you look at the past decade of progress, architecture contributed real gains, but the order of magnitude of those gains is small compared to what came from scaling data and compute. Transformer plus scaling got us the large models we have now, and the architecture itself has barely changed since 2017. That tells you something.

So how do I think about linear attention specifically? I'd split it into two levels.

The first level is efficiency. Standard attention is quadratic in sequence length, and the KV cache grows linearly, so for long context both compute and memory become the bottleneck. Linear attention, state space models, and similar designs give you constant memory and linear compute. On this level, I see architecture as serving the system. The job is to let the hardware run as close as possible to its full capability, and to let the inference economics work out. That's not a small thing, since the cost of serving long context decides which products actually exist, but it's an engineering tradeoff, not a change in what the model can do.

The second level is more interesting, and it's where I think most people get it wrong. The question is whether the architecture changes the model's capability ceiling, not just its cost. My current belief is that, for the pretraining paradigm, the ceiling is set mainly by data and scale, and most reasonable architectures converge to similar performance given enough of both. Linear attention pays a price in precise retrieval, which matters a lot for things like in-context learning and reasoning over long documents, and we don't yet have a clean way to recover that without hybrid designs that bring full attention back in.

But there's a deeper angle. If you look at where the next stage of capability comes from, I think it's less about pretraining and more about the model's ability to interact with an environment, to do very long horizon reasoning, to keep context that spans effectively unbounded lengths. Once you take that seriously, the memory question stops being an efficiency detail and becomes a capability question. A model with a fixed-size state has to learn what to remember and what to forget, which is something full attention never has to learn because it keeps everything. That sounds like a weakness, and under current training it mostly is. But it's also the only path to a model that can run for a very long time without the state blowing up, and compressing experience into a state is arguably closer to what intelligence actually requires.

So the way I'd put the relationship is this. Algorithms, meaning the training paradigm and the objectives, decide what a model can learn. Systems decide what it's economically feasible to train and run. Architecture sits in the middle and has to serve both, and whichever side is the bottleneck at the moment is the one architecture should bend toward. For the past few years the bottleneck was scaling, so the right architecture was the one that scaled most reliably, and that was the Transformer. Going forward, if the bottleneck shifts to long-horizon interaction and memory, then something like linear attention stops being a cost optimization and starts being part of the algorithmic answer.

What I'd caution against is pursuing architecture for its own sake. I've done that, and it produces papers but not progress. The architectural changes that actually matter are the ones that come from a clear understanding of where the real bottleneck sits, whether in the algorithm or in the system, and then removing exactly that one obstacle.

r001.rationale: The response says architecture must serve both algorithms and systems, and should bend toward whichever is the bottleneck.

r002.rationale: It does not argue that linear attention would be unnecessary when an algorithm avoids backpropagating through history.

r003.rationale: It does not suggest that success of a no-backpropagation approach would eliminate the distinction between training and inference phases.

r004.rationale: It describes linear attention's memory and compute efficiency but does not connect a separable recurrent structure to parallelizing next-token prediction.

astra-6.text:
I think architectural innovation is the link between algorithms and systems. An algorithm may look very efficient on paper, but whether it actually runs efficiently depends on how well it fits the hardware and the execution system.

Linear attention is a good example. It changes how attention is computed to reduce the cost of processing long sequences. But lower theoretical complexity does not automatically mean lower latency. You also have to consider memory access, parallelism, and how efficiently the operations can be implemented. And, of course, you have to ask whether the model preserves the quality you need.

So I would evaluate these innovations jointly: what capabilities does the architecture provide, how well can we train it, and how efficiently can we run it? The most valuable improvements come when those pieces work together. Systems constraints can inspire better architectures, and new architectures can open up opportunities for systems optimization.

sol-6.1.text:
I think architectural innovation is the bridge between algorithms and systems. An algorithm may look very efficient on paper, but whether it actually runs faster depends on how well it maps onto the hardware.

Linear attention is a good example. In principle, it reduces the quadratic cost of standard attention as the sequence gets longer. But lower computational complexity doesn’t automatically mean lower latency. You also have to consider memory access, parallelism, and whether the hardware can execute the operations efficiently. And, of course, you have to preserve model quality. If you need a larger model or more training to recover the quality, some of those savings may disappear.

So I wouldn’t evaluate an architecture only by its mathematical complexity or only by a benchmark on one device. I would look at the whole picture: training cost, inference cost, quality, and the workloads we actually care about. The most valuable architectural innovations change what is possible at that level. They give algorithms and systems a better place to meet.
